blocks.text: You get a request that sounds clear in the meeting, and two weeks later three people on your team have three different ideas of what the project is. When you run several projects at once, that kind of drift costs you hours you don't have, and it usually shows up right when a deadline is close.
In this guide, we'll show you how to write a project brief that keeps your team and stakeholders aligned before kickoff.
Here's what you'll get: what goes in a brief, six steps to write one, a fill-in template and tips for keeping every brief consistent across your projects.

A [project brief](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) is a short summary of the basic elements of a project. It lets your team share goals, strategy and timelines with stakeholders, and it should stay a high-level overview that leaves out unnecessary details.

[Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) describes the brief as one accessible place that outlines your project's goals, scope, timeline and target audience. Stakeholders and cross-functional collaborators get the key facts without wading through every detail.

[TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) puts the difference in plain terms: a project plan details how a project will get done, while a brief defines the who, what, when, where and why. If you're new to this kind of planning, our [project management basics](https://planwise.example/blog/project-management-basics) guide explains the wider picture and how a brief fits into it.

How long should a brief be, and does the length change with the size of the project? Both [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) and [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) say it can run from one paragraph to one page, depending on the project.

We suggest you follow TeamGantt and [aim for one page](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief), since people are more likely to reference a brief they can read in a couple of minutes. Here's why a short length helps when you run several projects:

items: Your team can read every brief quickly, even when several projects start in the same month.
Stakeholders can scan the brief and find the facts they need without asking you.

sections.h2: Why a project brief is worth the time

blocks.text: You might wonder if a brief is worth the extra step when your calendar is already full.

items: It gives your team information and clarity. Outlining the who, what, when, where and why gets people up to speed on the work and shows each person their role and how they can contribute, as [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) explains.

It builds a common understanding that reduces risk and confusion. If you're not doing a project charter, [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) says you can use the brief as a sort of agreement, reviewing scope and goals together and addressing any gray areas.

It rallies people before kickoff. Sharing the brief in a pre-kickoff meeting lets you introduce everyone involved and set a unified vision, which [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) says helps create a "We're all in this together" environment.

blocks.text: There is a fourth benefit that matters most when you run several projects at once. [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) calls a brief a central source of truth for key project information, so people know where to look instead of asking you.

Honestly, pointing people to one page can save you a lot of repeated questions over a busy month. When a teammate or stakeholder wants a quick answer about a goal or a date, you can point them to the brief.
Here's how that plays out in a normal week, from a new teammate's first day to your kickoff meeting. You can also use it as the agenda for your kickoff, so the conversation starts from shared facts.

sections.h2: What to include in a project brief

blocks.text: Most sources agree on a short list of must-have parts and then add a few extras that depend on your project. Here's how the lists compare, so you can pick what fits.
The core elements

Smartsheet says the three major elements of a brief are [a project overview, a goal statement and an estimated timeline](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief). Asana lists four elements, which are [background, objectives and success metrics, timeline, and target audience](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief).
If you want one starting point, you can combine the two lists into the steps below. Here's what that looks like:

items: Write an overview that says what the project is, why it is happening and the problem it solves.
State the goals and any success metrics, so the team knows what done looks like.
Add a timeline with a projected start date, an end date and the timing of major phases.
Name the target audience, so everyone knows who the work is for.
Give the background that stakeholders might not already have.

blocks.text: Extras worth adding when the project is bigger

Smartsheet notes that larger projects, or audiences who don't know your team, may need [background about your company, success metrics and the target market](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief). Raydyant adds a few more items to its brief: [the problem, the current situation, constraints, existing systems and how success might be measured](https://raydyant.com/blog/what-to-include-in-a-project-brief).

Smartsheet's simple template also covers [project name, purpose, goals, audience, story, team, budget and timeframe](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief-templates). Based on those sources, these are the extras we'd add when a project needs them:

items: Constraints, such as fixed dates or limits on people and tools.
Existing systems the work has to connect with.
A budget and the team members involved.
A plain description of how you will measure success.

blocks.text: You don't need an answer for every item on these lists, especially in the first draft of a brief. As Raydyant puts it, [the brief's job is to make the important questions visible](https://raydyant.com/blog/what-to-include-in-a-project-brief), so a short list of open questions is a fine thing to include.

sections.h2: How to write a project brief, step by step

blocks.text: Whether you write one brief a month or one a week, the steps below stay the same.

We reconcile the two views this way: write a first version early, before your internal kickoff meeting, and update it as details settle. Before you write, talk with your team and stakeholders about goals, timing and strategy, as [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) recommends.
1. Summarize the project and its purpose
Say what the project is, why it is happening and which problem it solves. One or two short paragraphs is enough for this part, and you can add detail later if the project grows.
2. State the goals and how you will measure success

List the concrete objectives and deliverables, as [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) advises. Then add [success metrics](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) so the team knows what done looks like.
3. Add background and your target audience

Give the context your stakeholders might not have, such as why you are doing this project and which business need it meets, as [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) suggests. Then name who the work is for, so every decision can be checked against that audience.
4. Name the key players and their roles
Introduce who is involved and what each person does, as [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) recommends.
5. List key deliverables with dates

Include a projected start date, an end date and the timing of each major phase and deliverable, as both [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) and [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) describe. A short dated list usually works better for the timeline section than a long paragraph does.
6. Add scope limits, constraints and other notes

State what is in scope and what is out, because naming the out-of-scope items is a simple way to head off scope creep. Then note your constraints and existing systems, which [Raydyant](https://raydyant.com/blog/what-to-include-in-a-project-brief) lists as useful context, along with any [other items of note](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief).

sections.h2: A project brief template you can copy

blocks.text: Here's a plain fill-in outline that you can paste into any document and complete for your next project. It pulls together the fields that the sources above agree on, so you can keep every brief in the same shape. Keep it to one page, as [TeamGantt suggests](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief), so people will actually use it.

items: Project name: [name of the project]
Purpose: [what the project is, why it is happening now and the problem it solves]
Goals and success measures: [the objectives you want to reach and how you will know you reached them]
Background: [the context a stakeholder might not have, such as the business need behind the work]
Target audience: [who the work is for]
Team and roles: [project owner, the people doing the work and who approves each stage]
Deliverables with dates: [each deliverable, the start date, the end date and the timing of major phases]
Scope: [what is in scope and what is out of scope]
Constraints and existing systems: [limits on time, budget or tools, and the systems the work must fit with]

blocks.text: This list follows the elements in [Asana's guide](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) and [Smartsheet's brief guide](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief). The simple template from [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief-templates) adds team, budget and timeframe, and [Raydyant](https://raydyant.com/blog/what-to-include-in-a-project-brief) adds constraints and existing systems.

You don't need every answer on day one, and a brief with a few open questions is still useful. As Raydyant notes, the brief's job is to make the important questions visible, so mark any gap as an open question and fill it in as details settle.
If you'd rather start from a ready-made version, we've built a [project brief template](https://planwise.example/templates/project-brief) that you can fill in and share with your team.

sections.h2: Project brief vs charter, plan and creative brief

blocks.text: Project briefs often get mixed up with a few similar documents, so it helps to know where each one fits. Most of them cover the same project from a different distance, so you pick the one that fits who needs the information.

We'll start with the project plan, since your brief gets compared to it most often. As [Asana explains](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief), a full project plan has seven elements, while your brief only needs four: objectives, timeline, target audience and scope.

A project charter is a different kind of document, and it serves a different purpose than the brief does. [TeamGantt says](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) a charter is longer and more formal, and it goes into the extra information you left out of the brief so you can secure approval. [Asana adds](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) that a charter formally authorizes a project.
The comparison below shows how the four documents differ, so you can see which one fits your situation.

An executive summary is the last document on the list, and [according to Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief), it suits expansive projects with C-suite stakeholders, while a brief suits cross-functional collaborators who need quick alignment.

Which of these documents do you need right now for the project that's waiting to start? If your team is waiting to start, a brief gets everyone moving, and you can add the longer documents later if the project calls for them.

sections.h2: Tips for keeping briefs useful across several projects

blocks.text: When you run several projects at once, a brief only helps if people actually open it. Here's how to keep every one of yours useful from the first week to the last.

items: Keep each brief to one page, because [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) says a short brief is something people will actually want to reference.
Keep it high level and leave out unnecessary details, as [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) advises.
Use one shared structure for every project, so stakeholders always know where to find the goals, the timeline and the team.
Refresh the brief whenever project details change, since [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) says a brief should stay as up to date as possible.
Condense the brief onto a single slide for your kickoff meeting, which [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) suggests as a quick way to share a project's key points.
Link the dates in your brief to a timeline view, such as a [Gantt chart](https://planwise.example/features/gantt), or to a board, such as a [Kanban board](https://planwise.example/features/kanban).

blocks.text: Why it works: a single page with the same layout every time means you spend your energy on the project instead of hunting for details. The shared structure matters most when you have five or six projects open and need to switch between them quickly.

What you can borrow: pick the layout from your most recent brief and reuse it for the next one. If a detail changes mid-project, update the one page and tell the team where to look, so nobody works from an old version.
You've read the steps, so now you can put them to work on a real project, because a brief you finish is worth more than a perfect one that stays in your head.
Here's how to start today:

items: Pick the project that starts soonest, because that one will benefit from a brief the most.
Open a blank page and fill in the six steps: the purpose, the goals, the background and audience, the key players, the dates and the scope limits.
Write what you know now instead of waiting for every answer.
Mark any gaps as open questions, since a brief's job is to make the important questions visible.

blocks.text: Next, share the draft at your kickoff meeting. [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) suggests using the brief to introduce everyone involved and build a unified view of the work.
When you share it, ask the team what is missing and what they would add.
Luckily, you don't have to build the layout from scratch, because we made a ready-to-fill version so every project in your queue can follow the same structure.
[Open the Planwise project brief template](https://planwise.example/templates/project-brief), fill it in for your next project, and share it at your kickoff.
What is a project brief for?

A project brief shares your project's goals, scope and timeline in a short document, so the team and stakeholders start with the same understanding. [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) describes it as a way to share goals, strategy and timelines with stakeholders. [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) adds that it clarifies each person's role, and [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) calls it a central source of truth for key project information.
How long should a project brief be?

Most briefs run from one paragraph to [one page](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief), depending on how big and complex your project is. [TeamGantt advises aiming for one page](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) so people will actually use it.
Who writes a project brief?

The project manager owns the brief and works with the team and stakeholders to settle the goals, timing and strategy, as [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) explains. [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) notes that your sales team or account manager might start a first draft, but the project manager makes sure it is complete and that everyone understands it.
What is the difference between a project brief and a project charter?

A [project charter](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) is longer and more formal, and it includes the extra details you left out of the brief so you can secure approval. [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) says a charter formally authorizes a project, while a brief is a high-level summary that keeps your team aligned on goals, scope and timeline.
What should a project brief include?

At a minimum, include an overview or background, your goals and success metrics, a timeline and your target audience, as listed by [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) and [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief). For larger projects, [Raydyant](https://raydyant.com/blog/what-to-include-in-a-project-brief) also suggests noting constraints, existing systems and how you will measure success, and it is wise to state what is out of scope.

cut.why: Sources give a range of one paragraph to one page; 'about one page' as best practice is only TeamGantt's advice and is stated here as general fact attributed to Smartsheet.
Describing TeamGantt as a 'project management software company' is not stated in the sources.

Smartsheet is said to suggest finalizing key details first (supported), but TeamGantt and Asana placing it 'at the very start' is partly supported; Asana says 'very beginning' and TeamGantt 'right at the start', so this is acceptable. Cut only if strict, but the stronger issue is none.
Smartsheet calls the overview section 'project overview' but does not frame it as this step; TeamGantt framing of who/what/when/where/why is supported, yet the sentence merges the two claims loosely.
The source says the project manager owns the brief and sales may start filling the template, which is supported; no issue, but the claim is attributed to 'the same page' ambiguously.
Table row about the brief's audience uses Asana's executive-summary comparison; claims are loosely mapped but not stated as a table in sources.
'Projects that need every element laid out in full' as the best-fit audience for a project plan is not stated in the sources.
'Projects that need formal sign-off' is an inference; sources say a charter secures approval and formally authorizes a project.
'Projects that include creative work' as audience is an inference; the source says the creative brief guides creative work.
'Some AI answers say 1 to 2 pages' cites AI answers, but the ChatGPT answer says approximately 1-2 pages while Gemini and AI Mode differ; acceptable, yet it is not from the numbered sources.
Storing the brief in a shared space is only from AI answers, not the numbered sources.
SMART goals come only from AI answers, not the numbered sources.
Claim that a new teammate can see purpose, people and timing from the brief on day one is an illustration not stated in sources.
Claim that you can update the brief in minutes is not stated in the sources.
